title: Gases
description: Pressure, the gas laws, mixtures, kinetic molecular theory, and why real gases deviate from ideal behavior.
overview: Gases are the simplest state of matter. Their particles are far apart and move almost independently, so very different gases obey the same few equations. That universality is why gas behavior is where chemistry first became quantitative: Boyle, Charles, Avogadro and Dalton worked out the laws in the 17th to 19th centuries, decades before atoms were accepted.
This chapter develops the ideal gas law from experiment, extends it to mixtures, explains it microscopically with kinetic molecular theory, and ends by examining how and why real gases fall short.
objectives: Convert among units of pressure and read a barometer or manometer.
Apply Boyle’s, Charles’s, Gay-Lussac’s and Avogadro’s laws and the ideal gas law.
Use PV = nRT for molar mass, density and reaction stoichiometry.
Calculate partial pressures with Dalton’s law, including gas collected over water.
Use kinetic molecular theory to find rms speed and apply Graham’s law.
Use the van der Waals equation and the compressibility factor to describe real gases.

sections.title: Gas pressure
body: **Pressure** is force per unit area, P = F/A. A gas exerts pressure because its particles collide with the walls of the container. The SI unit is the **pascal** (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²). Because the pascal is small, other units are common:

head: Unit
Value
table.caption: Pressure units. The torr and mmHg are equal for practical purposes.

body: A **barometer** measures atmospheric pressure by balancing it against a column of mercury. At sea level the column is about 760 mm high. A **manometer** measures a gas’s pressure relative to the atmosphere from the difference in heights of liquid in a U-tube. The mercury column’s pressure is ρgh, which is why a given height of mercury corresponds to a fixed pressure irrespective of the tube’s width.

Standard conditions are used to compare gases. In current IUPAC usage, **STP** is 273.15 K (0 °C) and 1 bar. Many textbooks still use 1 atm. State the convention when it matters. The molar volume of an ideal gas is 22.414 L mol⁻¹ at 273.15 K and 1 atm, and 22.711 L mol⁻¹ at 273.15 K and 1 bar.

body: Since n = m/M, the ideal gas law gives the density d = m/V = PM/RT, and a gas’s molar mass follows from a measured density: M = dRT/P. Gas density rises with molar mass and falls with temperature, so hot air rises and CO₂ pools in low places.

body: The ideal gas law supplies the missing link between the volume of a gas and the moles in a balanced equation. Convert the volume to moles with n = PV/RT, apply the mole ratio, and convert back if necessary.

sections.title: Gas mixtures and partial pressures
body: In a mixture of ideal gases each gas behaves as if it were alone. The **partial pressure** of a component is the pressure it would exert alone in the same volume. **Dalton’s law** states that the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures:
Air is 78.08% N₂ and 20.95% O₂ by volume (and so by mole), so at 1.00 atm the partial pressure of O₂ is 0.2095 atm. Mole fraction is the same as volume fraction for ideal gases.

example.title: Gas collected over water
example.problem: Oxygen is collected over water at 25 °C. The total pressure is 750.0 torr. The vapor pressure of water at 25 °C is 23.8 torr. What is the partial pressure of O₂?
solution: The volume of O₂ in an earlier example would be computed from this pressure, not from the total.

sections.title: Kinetic molecular theory
body: **Kinetic molecular theory** explains gas laws from the motion of particles. It assumes that: (1) gas particles are tiny compared with the distances between them, so their volume is negligible; (2) they move in constant random motion and collide elastically; (3) they exert no forces on each other except in collisions; (4) the average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature.

Pressure arises from the momentum the particles transfer to the walls. More collisions (higher density) or harder collisions (higher temperature) give more pressure. From these assumptions one derives PV = nRT and the key result that temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy:

eq: ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2) k_{B}T per molecule = (3/2) RT per mole

body: Here u_rms, the **root-mean-square speed**, is a typical speed, and M must be in kg mol⁻¹. At the same temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy, so lighter molecules move faster.

body.caption: Distribution of molecular speeds. Raising the temperature shifts the peak to higher speed and broadens the distribution.

body: The speeds follow the **Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution**: most molecules are near the typical speed, with a tail of fast ones. That tail matters for chemistry, because the few molecules with high energy are the ones that overcome an activation barrier.

example.title: Molecular speeds
example.problem: Compare u_rms of O₂ and H₂ at 298 K.
solution: H₂ is about four times faster: the ratio is √(32.0/2.016).

body: **Effusion** is the escape of gas through a tiny hole. **Diffusion** is the spreading of one gas through another. **Graham’s law** says the effusion rate is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass:

This is how ²³⁵UF₆ (M = 349) was separated from the slightly heavier ²³⁸UF₆ (M = 352): the lighter molecules effuse 0.4% faster, so thousands of stages are needed. Diffusion through air is much slower than effusion in a vacuum, since molecules collide about 10¹⁰ times a second with a **mean free path** of about 70 nm at 1 atm.

sections.title: Real gases
body: Real gases deviate from PV = nRT at high pressure, where the particles’ own volume matters, and at low temperature, where attractions matter. The **compressibility factor** Z = PV/(nRT) equals 1 for an ideal gas. Z < 1 means attractions dominate (the gas is more compressible than ideal), and Z > 1 means repulsion and molecular volume dominate.
The **van der Waals equation** corrects the ideal gas law for both effects:

The constant b accounts for the volume excluded by the molecules themselves, so the free volume is V − nb. The constant a accounts for attractions, which lower the pressure the walls feel, so the true pressure is increased by a n²/V² in the formula. Both are tabulated:

head: Gas
a (L² atm mol⁻²)
b (L mol⁻¹)
table.caption: van der Waals constants. Large a means strong attractions.

example.title: Ideal vs van der Waals
example.problem: 1.00 mol of CO₂ is held in 1.00 L at 300 K. Compare the ideal and van der Waals pressures.
solution: The real pressure is lower because CO₂ molecules attract one another, which outweighs the excluded-volume correction at this density.

body: Gases liquefy when attractions win. Above a **critical temperature** no pressure can liquefy a gas. The point where the real behavior is closest to ideal is at low pressure and high temperature, which is why He and H₂, with weak attractions, are the most ideal.

check.a: The volume excluded by the molecules themselves

summary: 1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 760 torr. Always use kelvin in gas calculations.
PV = nRT combines the Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac and Avogadro laws. R = 0.082057 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Density d = PM/RT. Molar mass M = dRT/P.
KMT: ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)RT per mole, and u_{rms} = √(3RT/M). Effusion rate ∝ 1/√M.
Real gases deviate at high P and low T. The van der Waals equation corrects for molecular volume (b) and attractions (a).
